Vitamin E has been used for the treatment of retinopathy of prematurity, p.1994. For discussion of the effect of vita- mins C, E, betacarotene, and zinc on age-related macular degeneration, see under Betacarotene, p.1931. HIV INFECTION AND AIDS. Low serum micronutrient concentra- tions are common in HIV-positive individuals, especially in the developing world; malabsorption, anorexia, diarrhoea, and increased energy demands contribute to malnutrition,1,2 which in turn contributes to immune impairment and in- creased mortality. Conflicting results have been found with the use of vitamin A in the prevention of vertical transmis- sion, see under Vitamin A, p.1974. A meta-analysis of trials of vitamins to prevent vertical transmission found no strong evidence of benefit and failed to exclude the possibility of harm, having included trials of vitamin A supplementation.3 A randomised trial found that multivitamin plus selenium supplementation increased CD4 and CD8 cell counts com- pared with placebo, but also unexpectedly increased the lev- els of genital HIV-1 shedding.4 Two other trials have also found that multivitamins, but not vitamin A, increased CD4 and CD8 cell counts;5,6 delaying the progression of disease in one,6 and decreasing adverse pregnancy outcomes in the oth- er.5 While some advise against vitamins as a therapy to pre- vent vertical transmission,3 and others recommend it as an ad- junctive treatment to antiretroviral therapy,1,2 most agree that in the setting of poverty and lack of adequate nutrition, provi- sion of food programs and/or supplementation along with antiretroviral treatment for HIV-infected individuals, is vital.7 1.
